tier_reason: First-party benchmark.js results in the README Performance section, from public code (bench/index.cjs, bench/suite.cjs, bench/data/assembly/static_aspr.ts, asc flags in bench/data/assembly/asconfig.json), but the CPU is given only as 'Intel Core i7 2.2 GHz (MacBook Pro 2015)' with no model and the Node.js version is not stated, so not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: AssemblyScript asc ^0.24.1 with optimizeLevel 3, shrinkLevel 0, converge, noAssert, incremental runtime, ESM bindings (bench/data/assembly/asconfig.json); protobufjs ^6.11.2 and benchmark ^2.1.4 (package.json); Node.js version not stated
corrections.workload: ts-proto's encode/decode/combined benchmark (bench/index.cjs, benchmark.js suite) on one small Test message (string, uint32, nested int32/int64/enum/sint32, repeated bool, double, float), with an as-proto case added that runs inside the wasm module
corrections.caveats: Mixed result: wins encoding (about 2.2x) and the combined case (about 1.3x), loses decoding by about 1.5x (889,283 vs 1,375,425 ops/sec for protobuf.js static); the README blames AssemblyScript's simple GC. The as-proto cases encode and decode a message pre-built inside wasm and discard the result, so they include no JS-to-wasm marshalling, while protobuf.js and google-protobuf encode a JS object; this matches as-proto's use from AssemblyScript code but is not a like-for-like JS API comparison. The payloads differ slightly: the AS message uses Enum.ONE (0, a proto3 default that is not written to the wire) and int64 682671883329470464, while bench.json uses enum 1 and int64 649545084044315. The README table has separate protobuf.js reflect and static rows, but the current bench/index.cjs runs only one protobuf.js (static) case, so the published numbers come from an earlier version of the script. Hardware is a 2015 laptop with no CPU model and no Node.js version; first-party only.

notes: Numbers on the README match the record exactly; baseline (protobuf.js and google-protobuf in V8) fits the category's JS-in-V8 baseline. Shortcomings for the orchestrator: decode slower than protobuf.js, in-wasm benchmark without boundary crossing, slightly different payloads, README numbers predate the current bench script, no CPU model or Node version; repo stale since 2023-03-24.

tier_reason: First-party README table produced by public code (benchmark/index.ts, benchmark/run.js; build flags -O3 --noAssert in package.json), but no hardware, CPU model or Node.js version is stated and each figure is a single timed call, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 200,000 strings: JS String += 11.93 ms, AS String += 7622.72 ms, StringSink AS 2.88 ms (about 4.1x over JS, derived from page data; README prints ~2600x over AS +=); 50,000 strings: JS 3.34 ms, AS 509.54 ms, StringSink 0.73 ms (about 4.6x over JS, derived from page data); 100 strings: JS 0.013 ms, AS 0.014 ms, StringSink 0.0042 ms (README prints 3x). The README headline 'up to 6 times faster than JS concat' and 'up to 4000 times faster than naive concatenation' exceed every row of its own table.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: AssemblyScript asc (devDependency ^0.27.0) -O3 --noAssert (package.json build:bench); Node.js version not stated
corrections.workload: Append n alternating 4-character literals ('foo|', '|boo') for n = 100, 50,000 and 200,000 and return the final length; one timed call per size with performance.now after 150 warm-up calls at n = 100 (benchmark/run.js, benchmark/index.ts)
corrections.caveats: Tiny first-party microbenchmark: no hardware, CPU model or Node.js version stated, and each figure is a single timed call (warm-up only at n = 100), so noise is unquantified. At 100 strings StringSink is about 3x faster than both plain concatenations (0.0042 vs 0.013 and 0.014 ms), but at that size all three are microseconds. The JS baseline returns res.length without flattening V8's rope while StringSink's toString() builds a flat string, which if anything favours JS. The headline 4000x is against AssemblyScript's own naive String +=, which copies the whole string on every append (quadratic), not against JS; the table's best is about 2,650x, and the 'up to 6x over JS' headline is not shown (best row about 4.6x, derived from page data).

notes: Numbers in the record match the README; the benchmark source was opened this time and is a plain append loop with a single timed call per size. Shortcomings: no hardware or runtime stated, single-sample timing, README headlines (6x over JS, 4000x) larger than its own table (4.6x, ~2600x); repo stale since 2023-02-17.

tier_reason: First-party README table (single browser timings) from the public demo harness examples/wasm_filter/www/index.html and src/lib.rs, with no browser, hardware or iteration count stated, so C; the claim is overstated and the timed SIMD invert path computes a different output from the baselines.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table (2.1 MB image, filter not named): AutoZig (Zig SIMD) 0.80 ms (2631.84 MB/s), Rust 2.50 ms (842.19 MB/s, '3.13x slower'), JavaScript 3.80 ms (554.07 MB/s, '4.75x slower'); headline '3-5x faster than pure JavaScript, 3x faster than Rust native'. Each figure is one click timed with performance.now, quantized to 0.1 ms. The example README (examples/wasm_filter/README.md) carries a different table for a 1920x1080 8.3 MB image (Zig WASM ~5 ms, pure JS ~25 ms, 'Canvas API' ~15 ms for invert) with a Canvas API row that has no implementation in the repo.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Zig -O ReleaseFast -mcpu=mvp+simd128 -fno-stack-protector, target wasm32-freestanding (engine/src/zig_compiler.rs; the example README still says ReleaseSmall); Rust wasm32-unknown-unknown with opt-level "s", lto = true and -C target-feature=+simd128 (examples/wasm_filter/Cargo.toml, .cargo/config.toml), built with wasm-pack --target web; browser and JS engine not stated
corrections.workload: Browser demo (examples/wasm_filter/www/index.html): one call of an RGBA filter (invert, grayscale or brightness; the README table does not say which) on a user-uploaded 2.1 MB image, timed with performance.now around a single call with no warm-up or repetition; the wasm rows include wasm-bindgen copy-in and copy-out of the Vec<u8>, the JS row allocates a new Uint8Array
corrections.caveats: Single-sample browser timings (one click, no warm-up, 0.1 ms timer granularity); browser, hardware and which filter was timed are not stated. The Zig SIMD invert_colors_raw subtracts every byte from 255, including alpha, while the Rust and JS versions and the example README ('Alpha channel unchanged') leave alpha intact, so the timed fast path produces different output (opaque pixels become transparent); the SIMD brightness path likewise changes alpha for negative deltas. A correct masked SIMD version would cost about the same, so the bug does not obviously create the speedup, but the row does not time the specified filter. The 'Rust native' baseline is a bounds-checked scalar step_by(4) loop built at opt-level "s" (size), so the 3x over Rust measures hand-written SIMD128 against a size-optimized scalar loop, not Zig against Rust; the grayscale filter is scalar in Zig too. The example README's second table (8.3 MB, ~5 vs ~25 ms, Canvas API row) has no matching code and looks unmeasured. Trivially vectorizable byte filter; crate autozig 0.1.2 with 80 downloads (crates.io, 14 recent); 5 stars; first-party only.

notes: Downgraded for an overstated claim and a correctness flaw in the timed path, tier stays C: the SIMD invert inverts alpha (baselines and the spec do not), Rust baseline is a scalar size-optimized loop, and every figure is one browser click. If the orchestrator reads the README table as the invert filter, D is arguable (timed fast path computes a different image), but the speed itself is not produced by the bug so this is not a reject.
